A tale of two contracts and a loan

A 386% growth number got me to open LiveWire’s filings. I went in looking for a denominator and came out with two manufacturing agreements, a services contract with a ninety-day trapdoor, and a loan that was quietly rewritten eight months before the quarter everyone is arguing about. The people at LiveWire have done real work. The paperwork has already decided how it ends.

00 — Why this brief exists

Who I am, and why I wrote this

A percentage got my attention. The contracts kept it. Here is how one led to the other.

I saw a number online: LiveWire, 386% unit growth in Q2. The number is accurate. It is also 55 motorcycles to 267, and fifty-five motorcycles is not a base, it is a parking lot. Anyone who has sat through a planning review has watched a percentage like that get built on a whiteboard, and normally it would be worth one paragraph and a shrug. What turned it into two weeks of reading was the trail it started. Open the 10-Q to find the denominator and you find a write-down that eats most of the gross loss. Ask why a company writes down brand-new inventory and you land in a manufacturing agreement priced cost-plus. Read that agreement and there is a second one, with KYMCO, signed the same day. Read the services contract that sits beside them and Harley-Davidson can walk on ninety days’ notice for no reason at all. And then, at the bottom of the pile, a loan that got its conversion feature removed and a lien over basically everything put in its place.

None of that is in the earnings release. None of it has been reported. It lives in the exhibits — the attachments nobody opens, including most of the people paid to cover the stock. That is the whole reason this brief exists.

The trail, in five documents

This is the order I read them in. Each one sent me to the next.

  1. Q2 2026 earnings release · 8-K, 23 Jul 2026
    386%. 55 motorcycles to 267. I went looking for the retail number the company itself calls its share measure and found it grew 171%, not 386%. Same table, different line.
  2. Form 10-Q · 5 Aug 2026 · segment note
    The write-down. About 87% of the quarter’s gross loss was a net realisable value adjustment on brand-new S2s. You don’t write down new inventory unless you paid more for it than it’s worth. So: who set the price?
  3. Contract Manufacturing Agreement · H-D · 26 Sep 2022
    Cost-plus. Harley builds, LiveWire buys into its own inventory at Harley’s cost plus a mark-up. Miss the volume and there is a provision for the parts Harley already bought — $6.1M of it, once, in 2023. And there is a second agreement, signed the same day, with KYMCO.
  4. Master Services Agreement · H-D · 23 Dec 2024 · §8.3(c), §8.4
    Ninety days. Everyone quotes the “forty percent” clause. The paragraph under it lets either party terminate for convenience on ninety days’ notice. No trigger required.
  5. Amended & Restated Term Loan · H-D · Nov 2025 · §1(c)(iii), §1(d)
    The seat change. Conversion feature gone. Security interest over substantially all assets in. First $10.0M of any ATM proceeds goes to Harley. $76.8M due 15 December 2027, compounding to about $85M. This was signed before the quarter above was even reported.

The paperwork, on one screen

Four instruments. If you read nothing else, read these cards; every section below is just the arithmetic they imply.

Contract manufacturing · Harley-Davidson
Cost-plus, buy-in
H-D builds the S2 at York. LiveWire buys every unit into its own inventory at H-D’s cost plus a mark-up, then writes it down to what it will sell for. Per-product minimum volumes start calendar 2027. Miss them and you pay for parts anyway.
26 Sep 2022 · amended 14 Feb 2024
Contract manufacturing · KYMCO
Take-or-pay, redacted
KYMCO builds the Honcho. Minimum Annual Volume Commitment per product, enforced by an Order Deficit Impact Fee. Five-year exclusivity on a maxi-scooter nobody has announced. Products, volumes and prices: Exhibit A, all [***].
26 Sep 2022 · restated 19 May 2026
Master services · Harley-Davidson
Ninety-day trapdoor
Either party can terminate for convenience on ninety days’ notice. The famous “forty percent” clause is the slower route, 180 days, and it turns on a word — “production” — the contract never defines. Seven-year term to end-2031, on paper.
23 Dec 2024 · effective 1 Jan 2025
Term loan · Harley-Davidson
Secured, no exit
$75M drawn Dec 2025. Conversion feature removed. Lien over substantially all assets. SOFR + 4%, compounding, nothing payable until 15 Dec 2027 — about $85M by then. First $10.0M the ATM raises goes to the lender. Covenants block asset sales and new debt.
Feb 2024 · restated Nov 2025 · drawn Dec 2025

I started with LiveWire because it is the only pure-play electric motorcycle company in the United States that has to file with the SEC. Everyone else in this category — Zero, Stark, Sur-Ron, Dust until it got bought — is private. Private means you get the numbers they feel like giving you. LiveWire has to file audited statements, attach its contracts and put the figures on the record whether they flatter it or not. That makes it the one place in this business where the press release can be checked against the arithmetic.

And the gap is the whole story. A quarter goes out as 386% growth; the filing shows 923 motorcycles in twelve months. A 76% market share gets claimed; three straight annual reports never say share of what. A new product is sold as the turnaround; the manufacturing agreement behind it commits the company to buy volume it has no way to move. None of it is hidden. It is just in documents most people never open, written by lawyers who are paid by the comma.

That is the hurdle I want to clear. Suppliers deciding whether to tool up for this category. Investors sizing a position. Dealers weighing a franchise. Engineers deciding where to put five years. Buyers wondering whether the company behind a $15,000 motorcycle will exist to honour the warranty. All of them are working off press releases, because the primary documents are long, dull, and written to be technically true rather than clear.

So I read them. All 260 filings for both companies, plus the manufacturing agreements, the loan documents and the exhibits nobody quotes. Then I show the work, link every figure to where it came from, and publish my corrections when I get something wrong. This is not an attack on LiveWire. It is an attempt to make the electric motorcycle market legible to people who have to make decisions about it — and to give them the same footing the manufacturers already have.

William Weppner

I spent most of my career inside the companies this brief is about. At Harley-Davidson I was the product manager for Touring, CVO and Trike — the lines that pay for everything else on Juneau Avenue. Before that I was sales planning lead for the CRF range at Honda and planning lead on the Grom — the bike that still defines the segment LiveWire is about to walk into — where registration data was something I worked in every day, not something I read about. Later I ran product development at Super73 and OEM sales at Sena, and I founded Faction MX, which I sold to private equity.

I race motocross at expert level and I ride constantly. That matters here for one specific reason: when this brief says what a motorcycle costs to build, what a dealer can actually retail in a season, or how much volume a segment will absorb, those are calls I made for a living — not things I inferred from a spreadsheet.

I write these because nobody else is doing this particular job. The financial analysts who cover this space don’t read manufacturing agreements. The powersports people don’t read 10-Ks. I do both, and the gap between what these companies announce and what they file is where the story usually is.

Standing and independence

I hold no position in LiveWire Group, Harley-Davidson, or any company named here — long, short, or derivative. I have no engagement, adverse or friendly, with any of them.

Where a conclusion rests on my time in the industry rather than on a filed document, I say so and give the basis. Where an earlier version of this brief was wrong, the fix is published in the log at §14 rather than made quietly. If something here is wrong, I want to hear it.

Part I

The growth

A number I saw online, and what it turned out to be measuring.

01 — The number

386% more motorcycles, and the loss did not move

Both numbers come out of the same table, the same segment, the same two periods. No outside denominator, no market definition, no room to argue about what got counted. This is the cleanest comparison in the filing, which is probably why nobody used it.

Unit sales, Q2 2025 → Q2 2026
+385.5%

55 units to 267. Average selling price basically flat: $11,400 to $11,483.

Operating loss, same two quarters
−0.2%

$(18,003) thousand to $(18,040) thousand. Five times the motorcycles. The loss got a hair worse.

Three qualifications, stated before anyone else states them

The base is the trough. Q2 2025’s 55 units is what makes 386% look impressive and what makes the flat loss look damning. Anyone using that quarter as a base — in either direction — picked a flattering comparison, and I include myself in that.

LiveWire has a legitimate explanation and it is in the same filing. Operating expense fell $967 thousand. Personnel came down $1,728 thousand on lower headcount; that saving got eaten by S4 Honcho development spend plus the costs of the Dust deal and the ATM programme. Reinvesting a cost-out into the next product is what a functioning company does. I have signed off on that trade-off myself.

The annual trend runs the other way, and it’s real. See below.

The other number: 76% market share

The same claim came with a second number: 76% U.S. market share. Seventy-six percent of what? Three annual reports later, nobody has written it down.

On the source of that figure

The most likely source is Motorcycle Industry Council registration data, which is the standard basis for U.S. two-wheel share and the thing every planning office in this industry lives on. MIC data is not public. It is a paid product that goes to reporting manufacturers and subscribers, and the model-level detail underneath it is available to OEMs and licensees, not to readers.

That has a direct consequence for this brief and for anyone reading the claim: the specifics cannot be independently verified. Not because the number is necessarily wrong — because the dataset it almost certainly rests on is one you cannot buy your way into, and LiveWire has published no definition next to it. So this section looks at what can be checked — whether a definition exists anywhere in the filings, and which measure the company itself nominates — and stops there.

First, the segment isn’t defined anywhere in the filings. The words “kilowatt” and “horsepower” do not appear once in LiveWire’s FY2025 Form 10-K. Whatever denominator produces 76% is a marketing construction with no disclosed basis in the company’s SEC reporting — which means it can’t be checked, and a share figure that can’t be checked isn’t a share figure.

That absence holds across three consecutive annual reports. FY2023, FY2024 and FY2025: no segment definition, no power threshold, and no mention of the Motorcycle Industry Council.

How a share figure of that size gets built — author's note

U.S. two-wheel share is generally measured from registration data the MIC compiles from manufacturer reporting. There is a structural feature of that dataset worth understanding if you have never worked with it: segment classification is declared by the manufacturer. Where a given model sits — dual-sport or enduro, standard or cruiser, on-road or off — is a decision the maker submits, not one an independent body assigns.

In product planning at Honda and at Harley-Davidson, my direct experience is that classification is treated as exactly what it is: a positioning decision, weighed with its effect on your reported competitive position in view. That is an ordinary, well-understood part of how the industry uses this data. It is also why a share percentage drawn from it means nothing without the segment definition stapled to it.

The arithmetic is unforgiving. Restrict a segment to on-road electric motorcycles above a power threshold and the U.S. competitive set narrows to a handful of nameplates. Set that threshold at 50 kilowatts and machines making 47 horsepower — the Can-Am Pulse and Origin, the most significant recent entrants — fall outside it entirely, while LiveWire’s own 63 kW and 75 kW products stay inside. The threshold, not the performance, decides who gets counted.

None of this is a claim about what LiveWire did. The company has published no definition, so no claim can be made either way. The point is narrower and it is enough: a share figure with an undisclosed denominator cannot be verified, and the mechanism by which such a figure gets made large is standard industry practice.

Second, the company’s own filing tells you which number measures share — and it isn’t the one in the post. From the Q2 2026 10-Q:

LiveWire Group, Form 10-Q, page 31

“Retail Motorcycle Unit Sales made through both the Company-owned dealership and Independent Retail Partners are a key measure of consumer demand and market share for LiveWire's electric motorcycles.”

So retail is the share measure, by the company’s own definition. Here is the table the 10-Q publishes:

Q2, motorcycle units20262025Change
Wholesale motorcycle unit sales25147+434%
Company retail motorcycle unit sales168+100%
Total LiveWire motorcycle unit sales — the 386%26755+385.5%
Independent Retail Partners, retail277100+177%
Total retail motorcycle unit sales — consumer demand293108+171.3%

The 386% is 94% wholesale — motorcycles shipped into the dealer channel, which is a revenue-recognition event and an invoice, not a customer. The number the company itself nominates as the measure of demand and share grew 171%. Anyone who has worked a month-end close at an OEM knows the difference between those two numbers, and knows which one gets put in the post.

To be fair to LiveWire on the point that actually matters: retail beat wholesale in both Q2 and the half — 293 against 267 in the quarter, 412 against 358 in H1. Dealer stock went down, not up. This was not channel stuffing, and the demand is real at its scale. But 386% and 171% are different claims about different things, and only one of them is about riders.

One day, two filings

The 386% quarter went out on 23 July 2026, in an 8-K under Item 2.02. That was the good news. The bad news arrived the same afternoon, by letter.

Same day, LiveWire got a letter from the New York Stock Exchange saying it was out of compliance with Section 802.01C — as of the 22 July close, the average price of its stock had been under $1.00 for thirty straight trading days. That letter was disclosed six days later, in a separate 8-K under Item 3.01.

The sequence, in the company's own filings

23 July — Q2 earnings release: unit sales up 386%. Same day: NYSE non-compliance notice received.
29 July — the delisting notice is disclosed by 8-K.
31 July — month end, and the first date on which the Exchange’s cure test can be applied. The stock closes at $1.81.
4 August — the board doubles executive severance and carves an H-D acquisition of 100% of the stock out of the definition of “change in control.”
5 August — the 10-Q is filed.

The stock roughly doubled on the earnings news, and then kept going — from a $0.77 close on the day of the release to an intraday $3.57 on 27 July, on 75.6 million shares against a normal day of under 200,000. Under Section 802.01C the price condition is cured if, on the last trading day of a calendar month, both the closing price and the preceding thirty-trading-day average are at or above $1.00. At the 31 July close of $1.81 the stock appears to have cleared it — nine days after the letter. The 386% headline is, quite literally, what got the company off the delisting track.

What is not filed: LiveWire has announced no return to compliance, and the 10-Q filed on 5 August doesn’t mention the letter at all. The cure reading above is mine, worked from the Exchange’s published standard and market closes; it is not a company statement. On the filings alone, the six-month cure period runs to 23 January 2027.

On the joint Harley-Davidson / AEA-Bridges call announcing the deal — filed with the SEC as a Form 425 — management put numbers on the record. I use them as the benchmark because the company picked them. Nobody made them say 100,000 units.

03 — Revenue

The business is smaller than the day it was sold

Revenue was $35.8 million in 2021, the year the deal was announced. Trailing twelve months to 30 June 2026: $31.3 million. The high-water mark was 2022, at $46.8 million.

Five years. An accumulated deficit of $337.4 million. And the top line is below where it started — against a plan that called for 51x. I have seen product plans miss. I have not seen one miss by the whole plan.

Part II

The lineup

From a $29,799 flagship to a $4,999 minimoto: the walk from premium to price and volume, and what each step cost.

Read it as a portfolio instead of a price list and the shape is a barbell with nothing in the middle. There is no LiveWire product between $5,000 and $11,000 — which is where two-wheel volume actually lives, and exactly where Can-Am parked the Pulse and the Origin.

A product that appears in no filing except one exhibit

The Amended and Restated Contract Manufacturing Agreement filed 22 May 2026 is with KYMCO, not Harley-Davidson. Its recitals name the covered product: “LiveWire’s Parisian maxi-scooter.” The two sides signed a memorandum of understanding on it dated 17 October 2024, for the joint design and manufacture of an EV maxi-scooter.

The words “Parisian” and “maxi-scooter” appear nowhere else in any LiveWire filing. Not a 10-K, not a 10-Q, not a press release. A fourth vehicle programme, under contract for nearly two years, exists in the public record only in the preamble of an exhibit. I have sat in enough product-plan reviews to know what a fourth platform costs a 150-person company. Nobody has been told it exists.

The agreement also puts LiveWire on the hook for a Minimum Annual Volume Commitment on each product, enforced by an Order Deficit Impact Fee: miss the number and you either take delivery of the shortfall or pay for it anyway. Supplier people will recognise that as take-or-pay. It sits alongside the per-product minimums owed to Harley-Davidson from calendar 2027. Exhibit A — the products, the volumes, the prices — is redacted in full. You can see the clip below.

Every pivot moved the price. None of them moved the overhead.

Two things fall out of that. First, the S2 is now selling at roughly the realised average the segment reports — $11,999 sticker against $11,483 recognised — which is what makes the net realisable value write-downs make sense: the cost-plus transfer price coming out of Harley-Davidson sits above where the market will clear the bike. Anyone who has run a transfer-price negotiation between an OEM and its own sub will know how that conversation goes.

Second, the Honcho is not another rung on this ladder. It is a different business. $4,999, built by KYMCO instead of Harley-Davidson, sold into the minimoto segment instead of the premium roadster segment — it shares a badge with the S2 and not much else. Dust points the same way: off-road, light, cheaper to homologate. Put those next to STACYC, the only segment that makes money, and the portfolio now describes a retreat from the premium on-road thesis that justified a $2.31 billion valuation.

Left to right, this is a company that vacated the top of its own map. The LiveWire ONE, once $29,799, now sits at $13,999 and is the most expensive thing the brand sells. Can-Am — which bought the Alta patents — brackets the S2 line from below on both the road and dual-sport rows.

And the Honcho does not land in open space. It lands inside the e-moto band, on top of Sur-Ron and Talaria machines that already own that price, while sitting $1,400 above the combustion Grom that outsells everything in the category. The one uncontested position on the map is the gap between $6,000 and $10,000 — which is where nobody, LiveWire included, currently builds anything.

05 — Precedent

Alta Motors, and the first time this happened

Before LiveWire was a public company, Harley-Davidson’s chequebook had already decided the fate of a different American electric motorcycle manufacturer.

DateEvent
March 2018Harley-Davidson takes a minority stake in Alta Motors, the Brisbane, California maker of the Redshift electric off-road and supermoto line, in a partnership to develop and produce electric motorcycles.
Autumn 2018Approximately six months later, Harley-Davidson ends the arrangement and elects to build its own Silicon Valley R&D operation instead.
18 October 2018Alta Motors ceases operations.
Early 2019BRP (Bombardier Recreational Products) acquires Alta's assets, including patents, stating no intention of reviving the brand.
2024–2026BRP is selling electric motorcycles under the Can-Am name. Harley-Davidson's electric business does not appear in Harley-Davidson's strategy.
Why this belongs in the file

The pattern isn’t that Harley killed Alta — Alta was a venture-funded startup with its own problems and companies fail for a hundred reasons. The pattern is narrower and better documented: Harley-Davidson’s decision to stop funding was, both times, the event that decided what happened next.

In 2018 that decision landed six months after the investment and Alta closed within weeks. In February 2026 it landed in an audited annual report: “The Company does not plan to make additional investments in LiveWire beyond the amount outstanding under the Term Loan.”

The difference this time is that it is a filed statement in a public company’s 10-K, with a maturity date attached and a security interest over substantially all of the borrower’s assets.

There is a second-order irony worth writing down. The Alta patents went to BRP, which now competes in the category. The Silicon Valley R&D centre Harley chose to build instead became part of the LiveWire business whose R&D spend has since dropped from $54.1 million to $23.9 million a year. Eight years and roughly $394 million of cumulative losses later, the electric motorcycle assets Harley-Davidson declined to buy are being sold by a competitor, and the ones it built are not named in its own five-year plan.

06 — Unit economics

Where the money actually goes

In Q2 2026 the Electric Motorcycles segment recognised $13,655 per motorcycle in total segment revenue — $11,483 of it the bike itself, the rest parts, accessories and apparel. Cost of goods sold was $23,172 per unit. Selling, admin and engineering was $58,049 per unit. Read those three numbers again. Then imagine trying to explain them to a dealer principal who just floored six of them.

What the write-down actually means

A net realisable value adjustment means LiveWire bought S2s from Harley-Davidson and immediately marked them down to what they can actually be sold for. Under the Contract Manufacturing Agreement those bikes are priced cost-plus — Harley’s cost, plus a mark-up.

The write-down is arithmetic proof that the transfer price is above what the motorcycle is worth on a showroom floor. The loss is real; it just gets booked at purchase instead of at sale, and it comes out of the contract, not the plant.

Part III

The contracts

Two manufacturing agreements and a services deal. This is where buying motorcycles became a losing trade and not buying them became expensive.

07 — The next product, and the paperwork behind it

The S4 Honcho meets a category ceiling

The S4 Honcho is priced: $4,999 for the Trail, $5,499 for the Street. It is built by KYMCO, not Harley-Davidson. Different plant, different country, different contract, and — this is the part that matters — a different set of minimums.

On the 23 July call, management said production had started and first units would hit authorised retailers later in the summer. So the Honcho contributed nothing to the 386% quarter and nothing to the trailing twelve months this brief runs on. Everything below is forward arithmetic on a product that has not yet sold a unit at scale.

Electric Motorcycles segment operating expense runs about $62 million a year. For that segment to get to operating breakeven on Honcho gross profit alone, you need somewhere between 46,000 units (at a 31% margin — the 2021 long-term target) and 103,000 units (at 14%).

The Honcho is a change in revenue mix, not a change in solvency.

At an optimistic 3,000 units and a 31% gross margin, the Honcho throws off roughly $4 million of gross profit against $62 million of segment operating expense — about 6% of the overhead. It walks into the segment 39% above the category leader’s price, with no nameplate, 105 dealers, and an electric powertrain carrying range and charging friction that a $3,599 gasoline Grom simply doesn’t have.

Note what has not changed. The 2021 plan promised ~100,000 units. After cutting cost per unit 47%, headcount 18%, and R&D from $54.1M to $23.9M, the volume needed to break even is still roughly the 2021 plan number. The cost-out was real. It didn’t move the bar.

How many Honchos keep the lights on?

“Afloat” is a cash question, not an accounting one. LiveWire burned $29.9 million in the first half of 2026 — call it $60 million a year. That is the hole the Honcho would have to fill on its own.

Contribution per unit is the variable. At a recognised wholesale price near $4,300, a KYMCO-built bike plausibly returns $500 to $1,500 a unit after landed cost, freight, warranty and dealer support. Those are the numbers a planner would pencil in before anybody in finance had seen the BOM.

The mid-case answer is roughly 50,000 to 120,000 Honchos a year, centring near 65,000. That is 70 times the company’s entire trailing-twelve-month motorcycle volume.

619 Honchos per dealer, per year. Twelve a week, every week, at every LiveWire dealer. I have run dealer allocations. Twelve a week is not an allocation, it is a Grom-shaped fantasy.

That is what 65,000 units across 105 dealers looks like. A typical powersports store retails a few hundred motorcycles a year across every brand and category it carries, and the ones that do a thousand are famous. And 65,000 units at $4,300 recognised is $280 million of revenue — nine times the company’s current total.

Run it the other way and it’s clearer still. At a realistic 3,000 units, the Honcho contributes about $2.7 million against $60 million of annual burn: 4.5% of the hole.

The likely case: roughly 2,000 units

Park the breakeven tables for a second and take the realistic number. On the segment evidence — a category leader doing about 10,000 a year with Honda’s network behind it, a new nameplate at a 39% premium, 105 dealers, and an electric powertrain in a segment that buys on price — roughly 2,000 Honchos globally in the first full year is a defensible estimate. It may be generous.

Basis for the 2,000-unit estimate

This number is mine, and it rests on having done the job rather than on a model. I held planning lead responsibility for the Honda Grom — the bike that defines this segment — and, as Sales Planning Lead for Honda’s CRF line, worked with Motorcycle Industry Council registration volumes as a primary planning input. That is the dataset that governs how U.S. two-wheel share is actually counted, and it is not public. Product planning at Harley-Davidson across Touring, CVO and Trike supplied the other half: what a dealer network of a given size can physically retail in a season.

The estimate reflects three things that dataset makes obvious. The minimoto segment is small and concentrated — the Grom isn’t the leader, it is very nearly the whole category. New nameplates without a service and parts footprint take years, not quarters, to register real volume. And 105 retail points cannot move what 1,000 can, no matter how good the bike is.

The estimate is not load-bearing. I give a number because a specific one is more useful than a vague one, and because the conclusion holds across a wide range: nothing under roughly 40,000 units changes any finding in this brief. If you think the Honcho does 8,000, you land in the same place.

At that volume the Honcho doesn’t just fail to help. It costs money in three separate ways, and two of them are in writing.

At ~2,000 unitsConsequence
1. It contributes almost nothing At $900 of contribution per unit, roughly $1.8 million — 3.0% of annual cash burn and 1.5% of the $121.8M that must be found by December 2027. Revenue of about $8.6 million against a company that needs orders of magnitude more.
2. It probably triggers the KYMCO deficit fee The KYMCO agreement obliges LiveWire to order at least the Minimum Annual Volume Commitment for each product, or pay an Order Deficit Impact Fee. The committed volumes are redacted — but a manufacturer tooling a new platform does not set them at 2,000. Selling well below commitment converts a growth product into a fixed liability.
3. It drops H-D below the 40% floor On the units reading of “production”: about 900 H-D-built motorcycles against 2,000 KYMCO-built ones is 31%. The threshold is crossed at roughly 1,350 non-H-D units. A modest Honcho success trips it; only failure keeps LiveWire compliant.
And the failure mode is already on the record — twice

Faced with a volume shortfall, the KYMCO agreement gives LiveWire a choice: pay the Order Deficit Impact Fee, or take delivery of the units needed to hit the commitment. Neither branch is hypothetical.

What buying motorcycles does. Under the Harley-Davidson agreement, H-D builds and LiveWire buys the bikes into its own inventory at cost-plus. On arrival they get written down to net realisable value. Roughly 87% of Q2 2026’s gross loss was that write-down. The FY2025 10-K says it without varnish, explaining why costs fell that year: “primarily driven by a significant decrease of the number of motorcycles purchased in 2025 as compared to 2024 resulting in lower net realizable value adjustments, as well as the effect of motorcycles that were purchased in 2024 and sold in 2025 that were already written down to net realizable value.” Margins improved because the company bought fewer motorcycles. Volume is what hurts.

What not buying them does. In 2023 LiveWire booked a $6,126 thousand provision for a liability for excess inventory components held by H-D under the terms of the Contract Manufacturing Agreement — parts Harley-Davidson had already bought to build motorcycles LiveWire didn’t take. That is the take-or-pay exposure working four years before the formal per-product minimums kick in.

So the calendar-2027 commitments don’t introduce a new risk. They formalise one that has already cost $6.1 million once, on a contract whose transfer price sits above the product’s market value — and the same structure now exists in duplicate with KYMCO.

Note on terminology, because I got asked: no motorcycles have been bought back from dealers. Retail sell-through beat wholesale in both Q2 and H1 2026. The write-downs are on inventory LiveWire owns, not returned stock.

Dust doesn’t change this on any near timetable. The assets were bought in May 2026; the Hightail was still in final validation with assembly in Bend, Oregon. Integration, tooling, homologation and dealer placement put meaningful volume in 2027 at the earliest, and off-road electric is not a high-volume category at that price. The one consolation is symmetrical: consideration is up to $14.75M but mostly contingent and payable in stock, so a programme that never scales also never pays out.

What the paperwork actually says

LiveWire signed two contract manufacturing agreements on the same day, 26 September 2022 — one with Harley-Davidson Motor Company Group, LLC, one with Kwang Yang Motor Co., Ltd. Services from Harley-Davidson run under a separate Master Services Agreement, amended and restated 23 December 2024, effective 1 January 2025, with a seven-year initial term running to the end of 2031.

That agreement is on file. Here is what its termination article says, and you can read it in the clip below the table.

ProvisionWhat it permitsNotice required
§8.4

And the KYMCO agreement, which is the heavier of the two

The Amended and Restated Contract Manufacturing Agreement with Kwang Yang Motor Co., dated 19 May 2026, is longer, longer-dated and more tightly bound than the Harley-Davidson deal. Its terms:

ProvisionWhat it does
§2.1
Exclusivity		LiveWire appoints KYMCO its exclusive manufacturer for the Covered Products for five years from the date KYMCO begins building them. The mirror image of the Harley arrangement — LiveWire is locked to KYMCO on this platform exactly as it is locked to H-D on the S2.
§2.1
Powertrain carve-out		Exclusivity “shall explicitly exclude the manufacture of the Powertrain which shall be manufactured by LiveWire through itself or its designee.” The motor and pack are the one thing LiveWire has not outsourced — and the only manufacturing asset it still controls.
§14.1
Term		Ten-year initial term, renewing automatically in successive five-year periods. Covered Product obligations cannot expire before their own five-year exclusivity runs out. Longer than the seven-year Harley MSA. The termination notice period in §14.2(b) is redacted.
§2.3
Take-or-pay		Minimum Annual Volume Commitment for each Product, enforced by an Order Deficit Impact Fee. Miss the volume and LiveWire either pays the fee or takes delivery of the shortfall. Reviewed annually. The committed volumes are in Exhibit A.
§14.3(ii)
The tax-credit lock		If KYMCO establishes U.S. facilities, equipment and labor qualifying for the associated EV tax credit and can build the product there, LiveWire loses the right to move that manufacturing away. The agreement anticipated LiveWire wanting U.S.-built product for credit eligibility and gave KYMCO a route to keep the work.
A product named once, in a recital

The Covered Product is identified in a single WHEREAS clause: “a Memorandum of Understanding on or about 17 October 2024 (the ‘Parisian MOU’) related to the joint design and manufacture of an EV maxi-scooter (‘Parisian’).”

The word “scooter” appears twice in the entire agreement, both inside that one sentence. Everything after it runs on the defined term “Covered Product,” which appears 24 times. Skip the recitals and you never learn what the product is — and no LiveWire filing, release or deck names it anywhere else.

One distinction to keep straight: the Covered Product carrying the five-year exclusivity is the Parisian. The S4 Honcho, if it appears at all, is a Product under the redacted Exhibit A — a weaker category. The minimum volume commitment in §2.3 attaches to “each Product,” so it very likely reaches the Honcho; the exclusivity architecture, though, was built around a scooter that has never been announced.

A correction to earlier revisions of this brief

Earlier drafts treated the 40% clause as the thing governing how much production LiveWire could move to KYMCO — and suggested it capped the affordability strategy at roughly a thousand units a year. Reading the agreement properly, that overstates it.

Section 8.4 lets either party terminate the entire Master Services Agreement for convenience on ninety days’ notice. Harley-Davidson doesn’t need the 40% trigger; it needs no reason at all, and convenience termination is faster than the 180-day route. The 40% clause is the narrower and slower of the two paths.

What the clause is genuinely evidence of is intent: in 2022, and again when the two sides re-papered the agreement in December 2024, both of them contemplated LiveWire moving manufacturing away from Harley-Davidson, and Harley wanted a documented trigger tied to it. Worth recording. Not a cap on the Honcho.

And “production” is not a defined term. The word appears exactly once in the agreement, lowercase, inside Section 8.3(c). There is no capitalised definition of “Production” anywhere in the document. A termination right turns on a word the contract never defines.

My read, offered as industry interpretation and not contract text: in Harley-Davidson’s internal product-planning vernacular, “production” means motorcycles built at the plant — unit output, not revenue and not platforms. I used the word that way in planning meetings for years. On that reading the test is a unit-count ratio of H-D-built motorcycles to LiveWire’s total motorcycle production, and STACYC balance bikes fall outside it. That is the most natural reading of an undefined term, but it is an interpretation, and the agreement doesn’t supply it.

Nor does cutting solve it

The obvious counter is to shrink the company to fit the product. Run it: at 3,000 Honchos and $900 of contribution, plus roughly 1,000 S2 units at around breakeven and STACYC’s small operating income, total operating expense would have to fall to under about $5 million a year to reach cash neutrality. Electric Motorcycles segment operating expense is currently $62 million.

That is not a cost-reduction programme. That is a description of a much smaller company that no longer designs motorcycles — and it wouldn’t service the $76.8 million due in December 2027 either.

The conclusion falls out of the arithmetic, not out of any opinion about the bike: there is no combination of Honcho volume and cost cuts that reaches solvency at a scale this category can supply. Which is why the resolution, when it comes, will be financial rather than commercial.

Part IV

The loan

A date that cannot be moved, and the instrument that decided who is on which side of the table.

08 — The clock

Cash, and a date that cannot be moved

Cash burned in H1 2026: $29.9 million. The 10-Q asserts roughly twelve months of runway from issuance — call it August 2027. The Harley-Davidson term loan, $76.8 million secured on substantially all assets, matures 15 December 2027.

And what would it actually take to pay it back?

Six quarters separate 30 June 2026 from 15 December 2027. At the current rate the company burns about $15 million a quarter. And the debt is growing: no interest is payable until maturity, so the $76.8 million carrying value at 30 June accretes at SOFR plus 4.00%, compounded semi-annually. At the rate accrued in H1 2026, the December 2027 payoff is closer to $85 million.

135,000 Honchos in fourteen months. Twenty-one per dealer, per week.

That is 13.5 times the Honda Grom’s entire annual U.S. volume, squeezed into a bit over a year, by a company that sold 923 motorcycles in the last twelve months through 105 dealers — and the Honcho isn’t shipping in volume yet.

The at-the-market programme is the only other lever on the balance sheet, and it isn’t one — for a reason buried in the loan agreement. The Term Loan requires that the first $10.0 million of net ATM proceeds go to prepaying Harley-Davidson. LiveWire has paid $800 thousand of that so far. Until $10 million has been routed to the lender, the ATM raises no usable cash at all. It is an ATM that pays the bank first. The clause is below.

Past that, $48.4 million is undrawn, covering under 40% of the gap even if fully placed — and placing it means issuing roughly $48 million of stock into a float of about 44 million shares at $1.16, which isn’t a financing so much as a description of what would happen to the share price.

The company has said when it is looking

The 10-Q filed on 5 August 2026 doesn’t leave the timing open. On liquidity, it says management “will continue to actively pursue additional financing during the third quarter of 2026,” and that if the Company can’t secure capital in the amounts needed, on acceptable terms, or at all, “it could adversely affect its ability to satisfy obligations as they become due and execute its strategic business objectives.”

That quarter ends on 30 September 2026. This isn’t a 2027 problem being managed at leisure; it is a stated intention to raise money inside a window now measured in weeks. What that raise looks like — ATM, a new instrument, or something from Harley-Davidson — is the most informative thing that will happen to this company in the near term, and it will arrive as an 8-K.

What the number is actually telling you

Nobody at LiveWire or Harley-Davidson expects this note to be repaid out of motorcycle sales, and I don’t suggest anyone thinks otherwise. The arithmetic is worth doing precisely because the answer is unreachable: it establishes that the December 2027 maturity gets settled by a financial decision, not a commercial one.

Harley-Davidson holds both the secured note and roughly 78% of the equity. It is on both sides of that decision, and the range of outcomes — extension, conversion, exchange, sale, or something else — is largely its to pick. No filing says what it intends, and I don’t assert one.

09 — Analysis, not reporting

What a financial resolution could look like

Read this section differently

Every section before this one is sourced to a filing, a company release, or a manufacturer’s published price. This one isn’t. It lays out the mechanisms available to the parties under instruments already on file. It assigns no probabilities and it states no intention on anyone’s behalf.

No filing says Harley-Davidson intends to divest, wind down, convert, acquire, or take private its interest in LiveWire, and nothing below should be read as suggesting one of those has been picked. The closing outlook is my judgment, and it says so.

The repositioning, in dated instruments

Read alone, each of these is routine corporate housekeeping. Read in order, they describe one thing.

DateInstrument or statement
14 Feb 2024H-D extends a $100M Convertible Delayed Draw Term Loan. If LiveWire cannot repay at maturity, H-D converts to equity. That is a parent's instrument — an equity backstop. It is never drawn.
9 Nov 2025Amended and restated. The conversion feature is removed. A security interest over substantially all assets is added. So are negative covenants blocking asset sales, new debt, liens, investments and fundamental changes. And the first $10.0M of any ATM proceeds is redirected to the lender.
15 Dec 2025$75.0M drawn. Interest accrues at SOFR + 4.00%, compounding semi-annually, nothing payable until maturity.
26 Feb 2026H-D's audited 10-K: “does not plan to make additional investments in LiveWire beyond the amount outstanding under the Term Loan.”
5 May 2026“Back to the Bricks.” Six financial targets, none of them LiveWire. The word “electric” does not appear.

In fifteen months, Harley-Davidson went from parent to secured creditor. It didn’t leave the table. It changed seats.

Every step above is a filed instrument with a date on it. What the sequence means is interpretation; that it happened is not. And the direction never wavers: an equity backstop got swapped for a secured claim, the borrower’s ability to sell anything or restructure got fenced in, and the only equity-raising mechanism it has left was made to pay the lender first.

One thing the author does not claim to know

Why the conversion right was removed. Two readings fit the same facts. A lender expecting to be repaid or refinanced has no use for a conversion feature and would reasonably drop it. A lender who would rather hold a secured claim over the assets than a diluted stake in the equity would drop it for the opposite reason.

The distinction matters — it’s roughly the difference between an extension and a foreclosure — and nothing on file settles it. Anyone claiming to know which is guessing.

One structural fact drives the whole set. Harley-Davidson holds both the secured note and roughly 78% of the equity. In an ordinary distressed situation a creditor negotiates with shareholders; here they are the same party. The only outside interest with anything at stake is the ~22% public float.

MechanismHow it worksWhat it costs H-D
Extend or amend the note Maturity pushed beyond December 2027, possibly repriced or re-covenanted. Threads the “no additional investments” language, since extending an existing note is not new investment. Nothing today. Preserves every other option.
Convert debt to equity Correction worth noting: H-D used to hold this as a contractual right. The February 2024 Convertible Delayed Draw Term Loan let H-D convert amounts outstanding to equity at maturity if it determined, reasonably and in good faith, that LiveWire lacked the financial wherewithal to repay. That facility was never drawn, and the November 2025 amendment and restatement removed the conversion feature. A conversion today would require a fresh negotiated agreement, not the exercise of an existing right. The arithmetic if it happened: at $1.20, $85M is roughly 71 million shares, taking H-D from ~78% toward ~88%. Delaware's short-form merger provision becomes available at 90% — above which a parent may squeeze out minority holders without a shareholder vote. No cash. Dilutes the minority substantially.
Harley's consent right over all of it The Term Loan carries negative covenants restricting LiveWire's ability to incur indebtedness, create liens, sell assets, make investments, make fundamental changes, pay dividends, or enter into affiliate transactions. Selling STACYC, raising senior money, or merging with anyone plausibly requires the lender's agreement. Nothing. It already holds it.
Take-private Acquire the float. Requires a Schedule 13E-3, a special committee of independent directors, and a fairness opinion — the function the conflicts committee described on the 2021 investor call was created to perform. ~$54M at market, and minority squeeze-outs typically carry a 30–50% premium. Less than another year of funding.
Sale to a third party KYMCO is the structurally obvious counterparty — existing shareholder, manufacturer of the volume product, short on Western brand and distribution. Complicated by the secured note sitting ahead of all other claims. Recovers something; crystallises the loss.
Break-up STACYC is separable and profitable — 45.6% gross margin and positive operating income in Q2 2026. It would sell readily. Selling it also removes the only profitable segment and makes the remainder strictly worse. Raises cash. If STACYC is sold, the remainder is being prepared for wind-down, not growth.
Outside capital Named directly in H-D's own risk factor: “the ability of LiveWire to obtain sufficient funding from sources other than the Company.” A new investor would face a $75M annual loss, a secured creditor ahead of them, and a 78% controlling holder above them — and would likely require H-D to subordinate or convert first. Nothing, but routes back to conversion.
Secured-creditor remedies The note is secured by substantially all assets. On default, foreclosure — or a reorganisation with H-D as debtor-in-possession lender and stalking-horse bidder — transfers the assets and leaves the public equity behind. A documented legal right, recorded here for completeness. Recovers assets. Wipes out the minority.
Delisting Compliance is fragile: the shares were non-compliant with NYSE Section 802.01C as recently as July 2026 and trade at $1.16 as of 3 September 2026. A move off the exchange reduces the cost of being public and destroys what the 2022 business combination was for. Nothing. Passive.

The incentive that probably sets the timing

Every financial target in “Back to the Bricks” is an HDMC target — EBITDA above $350M by 2027, 25–30% gross margin, operating expense under 20% of sales. LiveWire’s $70–80 million annual drag doesn’t show up in those metrics, but it does show up in Harley-Davidson’s consolidated results. Anything that deconsolidates LiveWire improves the reported picture at the cost of crystallising the loss. That tension — reported earnings against a one-time write-off — is the most plausible driver of when, whatever the what turns out to be.

What to watch, in order of information value

Filing or eventWhat it would indicate
SC 13E-3, a special committee announcement, or a 13D/AA take-private in motion. Note that no Schedule 13D has ever been filed on LiveWire — its appearance would itself be the news.
8-K recording a share issuance to H-D; share count jumpsDebt conversion. Check immediately whether it crosses 90%.
8-K amending the credit agreementExtension. The date moves; nothing else does.
8-K disposing of STACYCBreak-up. The strongest single signal in the set.
SC 13D by a new party, or a merger agreementThird-party sale.
Forbearance language, or a going-concern qualification in the FY2026 10-KThe distressed path.
A new NYSE deficiency notice, or a Form 25Delisting.
Aggressive ATM drawdownDistress. Only 3.2% of the $50M programme has been placed — and the first $10.0M of net proceeds goes to Harley-Davidson before LiveWire sees a dollar. Heavy use at these prices would be a decision made under pressure.

The Harley-Davidson read-through

LiveWire is a $247 million company with a 44-million-share float. Harley-Davidson is a $27.81 stock that actually trades. For most readers the bigger question isn’t what happens to LiveWire — it is what LiveWire is doing to the parent’s reported numbers, and what changes if it stops.

Harley-Davidson consolidates LiveWire and reports it as one of three segments alongside HDMC and HDFS. That means LiveWire’s losses run straight through H-D’s income statement, reduced only by the share attributed to LiveWire’s minority holders.

Q2 2026, from both filingsAmount
LiveWire net loss (LVWR 10-Q)$(18,213)K
Loss attributed to noncontrolling interests (HOG 10-Q)$(824)K4.5%
Borne by Harley-Davidson$(17,389)K95.5%
H-D net income attributable, as reported$79,805KEPS $0.75
Same figure with LiveWire's loss removed$97,194K+21.8%
An anomaly worth flagging — and not explaining away

Harley-Davidson owns roughly 78% of LiveWire. On a straight ownership split, the minority would eat about 22% of the loss — some $4.0 million in the quarter. The filed figure is $824 thousand, or 4.5%.

So Harley-Davidson is carrying about 95% of an economic loss in a company it owns 78% of. There are ordinary accounting explanations — loss attribution once minority equity is exhausted, basis differences, the elimination of intercompany manufacturing margin — and I don’t claim to know which applies. The figures are here because both are filed and the gap between them is large. Working out the cause needs H-D’s equity roll-forward and is beyond this brief.

On the half year the effect is bigger. LiveWire’s H1 net loss was $36.3 million; $1.5 million went to minority interests. Strip out the remainder and H-D’s net income attributable goes from $104.6M to $139.4M — a third higher — and first-half diluted EPS from $0.97 to roughly $1.33. Annualised, LiveWire is worth on the order of $0.65 of Harley-Davidson EPS.

What that arithmetic does not say

Removing a loss is not the same as deconsolidating a business. Three things sit between the calculation above and any real outcome, and all three cut against it.

Harley-Davidson makes money from LiveWire. It builds the bikes cost-plus with a mark-up, charges a monthly services fee, floors the dealers through HDFS, and now collects interest at SOFR + 4%. Those revenues leave with the customer. The net benefit of separation is smaller than the loss it removes — possibly a lot smaller.

Deconsolidation crystallises a charge. H-D carries an investment in LiveWire and a $76.8 million secured receivable. What comes off the balance sheet, and at what value, isn’t derivable from LiveWire’s filings — it needs Harley-Davidson’s own carrying value, which this brief hasn’t established.

And the targets already exclude it. Every financial target in “Back to the Bricks” is an HDMC target — EBITDA above $350M by 2027, 25–30% gross margin, operating expense under 20% of sales. LiveWire never appears in the metrics management is measured against, but it does appear in the consolidated results shareholders get paid on. That gap is the whole tension.

Which reframes the question for anyone holding HOG rather than LVWR. Harley-Davidson is currently absorbing roughly $70 million a year of losses, and about $0.65 of annual EPS, from a segment that is absent from its own five-year plan and whose funding it has publicly capped. The strategic decision has already been made and disclosed. The accounting hasn’t caught up. When it does — by sale, deconsolidation, restructuring or write-down — the reported numbers move, one way on earnings and possibly the other way on a one-time charge.

Ground Truth No. 02 takes up the parent directly: Harley-Davidson’s carrying value of LiveWire, the write-off arithmetic, and whether the Back to the Bricks targets are reachable on HDMC alone.

Outlook — my judgment

The commercial question is already settled, and arithmetic settled it, not execution. Clearing December 2027 on product needs roughly 135,000 Honchos in about fourteen months, in a segment whose best-selling bike does 10,000 a year with Honda’s dealer network behind it. No plausible ramp closes that. The Honcho may well be a good motorcycle; it cannot be a solvency event.

At the realistic figure — on the order of 2,000 units globally — the position is worse than neutral. The Honcho would contribute about 3% of annual cash burn, probably incur a deficit fee against a minimum it can’t meet, and push Harley-Davidson below the 40% manufacturing floor. The distance between the volume that saves the company and the volume the category can supply isn’t a difference of degree. Nothing below roughly 40,000 units changes a single conclusion in this brief.

So the financial question is the only live one, and one party decides it. Harley-Davidson holds the note, the security interest over substantially all assets, roughly 78% of the equity, the board, the covenants restricting asset sales and fundamental changes, the manufacturing, the dealer financing through HDFS, the building, and a services agreement it can cancel for convenience on ninety days’ notice. If you are looking for the counterparty with leverage, there isn’t one. The public float has a ticker symbol and a very good view.

Timing points to the first half of 2027. The 10-Q asserts roughly twelve months of runway from issuance — about August 2027 — and the note matures 15 December 2027. Those converge. Something forces the question earlier still: the FY2026 10-K lands around February 2027, and an auditor has to take a going-concern view with nine months of cash against $85 million coming due.

Base case: extension or restructuring on Harley-Davidson’s terms. It is the cheapest path, it keeps every other option open, it produces no write-off headline, and Harley controls both sides of the table. The tell would be an 8-K amending the credit agreement.

What would genuinely surprise me is outside capital. The security interest and the covenants make LiveWire close to unfundable by anyone willing to rank behind Harley-Davidson — which is the practical meaning of the risk factor about obtaining funding “from sources other than the Company.”

A complication nobody has priced. Four vehicle programmes are now in flight — the S2 platform, the S4 Honcho, the acquired Dust line, and the undisclosed Parisian maxi-scooter — carrying minimum-volume commitments to two separate manufacturers, on a $23.9M annual R&D budget and roughly 150 people. I have watched OEMs with ten times the headcount struggle to carry four platforms. That is a great deal of committed forward spend for a company whose funding was capped in February 2026.

What this brief does not conclude

That LiveWire fails. A controlled restructuring by a parent that owns 78% of the equity isn’t a failure event for the business; it is a change in who owns it and on what terms. The people running the company cut cost per motorcycle 47% in two years, improved operating cash burn 18.4% year over year, run a profitable STACYC segment, and rebuilt a dealer network they had cut by 30%. That is execution, and I have seen far worse from far bigger companies.

What the filings describe is not a company being run badly. It is a company whose structural position was fixed in place by the end of 2025, and whose remaining decisions belong to someone else. What follows is the tape, the scorecard, and then the people who did the work anyway.

Part V

The tape

What the market did with all of this, and what the people inside did with the market.

10 — The tape

What the stock did, and what insiders did with it

Four years of share price, every reported insider trade laid over it. No names — the pattern is the point, not the people.

Three things stand out on that chart before you read a word of the filings. The line goes from about $10 to $1.16. The circles only ever appear on the way up — on the spikes, not the troughs. And there is one kind of mark that never appears at all.

All Forms 3, 4, 4/A and 5 filed under CIK 0001898795, 26 September 2022 to 3 September 2026, parsed from the SEC’s XML: 134 ownership filings, 141 reported transactions, 16 officers and directors. Two amended transactions counted once. Value is shares × reported price.

In four years as a public company, no officer or director of LiveWire has bought a single share on the open market. Not at $10, not at $12.29, not at $0.65. It is more common than it should be — people paid in stock rarely buy more — but it is the one signal in this brief that costs nothing to send and has never been sent.

The selling is not spread out either. Only seven months in four years contain any insider sale at all, and two of them — June 2025 and July 2026 — account for 81% of the shares and 76% of the proceeds. Both months follow the same event: a retail-driven spike with nothing from the business behind it. In the week of 25 May 2025 the stock went from $1.01 to $4.50 on 220 million shares; over the next fortnight seven insiders sold $2.07 million at $5.50 to $8.60. In the fortnight from 19 July 2026 it went from $0.66 to an intraday $3.57 on 233 million shares — the 386% release was the spark — and in the three days after, four insiders sold $776 thousand at $1.98 to $2.38. The second window also happens to be the week the company disclosed the NYSE letter it had been holding since the day of the release.

What the record supports, and what it doesn’t

The calendar was clean. The delisting letter was disclosed inside the four business days the rule allows. The July sales sit inside the trading window that normally opens after results. Nothing about the timing was irregular, and nothing here alleges otherwise.

The timing was a choice. Not one of the 38 sales in four years was made under a Rule 10b5-1 plan — the box is on every Form 4 and it is zero on all of them. And the July lots had not just vested: the Forms 144 show them acquired between six weeks and two and a half years earlier, held through every prior window, and sold in the single week the stock traded above $2. That is not evidence of anything improper. It is evidence of price sensitivity, and it tells you what the people with the best information thought their own stock was worth at the moment retail was paying triple.

They are still long. Every one of the July sellers retains far more in unvested units than they sold — in the largest case roughly six times as much. Nobody exited. They took a slice of a liquidity window that had not existed the week before.

And the timing has been good. Of the 38 sales, 36 were followed by a lower price six months later. In a stock down 88% since the merger that requires no foreknowledge; it is what selling into strength looks like when the trend only goes one way. It closed at $1.16 on 3 September.

Part VI

The final word

What was promised, what was delivered, who did the work, and who holds the pen.

Where the forecast actually lives

People ask me where LiveWire publishes its unit guidance, and the honest answer is: mostly, it doesn’t. LiveWire’s own 10-K has never contained a forward volume number — it is risk factors and history. The number lives one floor up, in Harley-Davidson’s annual report, as a single paragraph in the MD&A Outlook, wedged between the HDMC margin guide and the HDFS guide. LiveWire then repeats it in the “Financial Outlook” bullets of its earnings-release 8-K. Four annual reports, four paragraphs, clipped below in order. Watch the unit number: 750–2,000, then 1,000–1,500, then 1,000–1,500 again, then gone.

The pattern, in one sentence

LiveWire hits its spending numbers and misses its volume numbers, every year, without exception. The operating-loss guidance was met in 2023, beaten in 2024, and met in 2025 after two revisions. The unit guidance was missed in 2023, missed in 2024, withdrawn in 2025, and not offered at all in 2026. That is not a company that can’t manage. It is a company that can control what it spends and cannot control what it sells — and the 2021 plan it was sold on was a volume plan.

The one number that has never moved is the deadline. 2026 was the year everything was supposed to happen. It is 2026.

12 — Credit where it’s due

The people did the work. The paperwork didn’t.

I have spent most of this brief on contracts and a loan. Before the final word, here is what the people inside LiveWire actually pulled off — each one filed, each one real, and each one followed by the reason it still isn’t enough. That second line is the whole story of this company: it is not a lineup problem the engineers can fix or a demand problem the dealers can fix. It is a structure problem, and structure lives in exhibits.

−47%
Cost per motorcycle · 2024 → Q2 2026
$44,147 to $23,172 a unit in two years. That is real engineering, real sourcing, and real fights with suppliers. Nobody hands you that.
Why it isn’t enoughCost of goods is still $23,172 against $11,483 recognised per bike. Halving the cost of a thing you sell at a loss still leaves a loss.
−61%
Loss per unit · two years
Operating loss per motorcycle came down from an almost theoretical number to $67,566. The direction is right and the pace is fast.
Why it isn’t enoughAt $67,566 a unit, every motorcycle sold moves the company further from December 2027, not closer. The overhead does not scale down with the sticker.
−18.4%
Operating cash burn · H1 2026 vs H1 2025
Net cash used in operations fell from $32.4M to $26.4M. On a company this size that is a genuine, disciplined outcome.
Why it isn’t enough$26.4M a half is still $52.9M of cash against about $85M due in fifteen months. Better burn extends the runway by weeks, not by a maturity.
45.6%
STACYC gross margin · Q2 2026
Revenue $5,469K, gross profit $2,495K, positive operating income. The balance-bike business is a real business, and it is the only segment that makes money.
Why it isn’t enoughIt is a few million a year of operating income against $62M of Electric Motorcycles segment opex. It is also the most saleable asset in the building, and the covenants restrict selling it.
171%
Retail sell-through · Q2 2026
Retail beat wholesale in Q2 and H1: 293 vs 267, 412 vs 358. Dealer stock went down. This was not channel stuffing. The demand is real at its scale.
Why it isn’t enoughIts scale is 923 motorcycles a year. The plan of record was 100,000. Real demand at one percent of plan is still one percent of plan.
105
Dealers · 88 → 96 → 105
They cut the network 30%, then rebuilt it: 88 at end-2024, 96 at end-2025, 105 at 30 June 2026. Rebuilding a network you just cut is harder than building one.
Why it isn’t enough105 doors cannot retail what 1,000 can. Every breakeven number in this brief divides by 105, and that is why they come out as twelve, twenty-one, thirty-eight per dealer per week.
$23.9M
R&D · down from $54.1M
R&D from $54.1M (2023) to $23.9M (2025), headcount 182 to about 150 — while starting the S4 Honcho and closing the Dust deal. That is a small team carrying a lot.
Why it isn’t enoughFour platforms — S2, Honcho, Dust and the undisclosed Parisian — now sit on that budget, with minimum-volume commitments to two manufacturers. Discipline is not the same as capacity.
$4,999
S4 Honcho · built by KYMCO
They got a new platform, at a new price point, from a new manufacturer, into production in the middle of all this. Launching anything under these conditions is an achievement.
Why it isn’t enoughIt is a minimoto walking into the Grom’s segment at a 39% premium, with a take-or-pay minimum behind it. At any plausible volume it costs money. At 135,000 units it clears the loan. Nothing in the middle exists.

All figures from LVWR Form 10-K FY2025 and Form 10-Q Q2 2026, and the Q2 2026 earnings release; per-unit figures are arithmetic on filed numbers as shown in §06. The 2021 plan of record is from the Form 425 of 14 December 2021.

So here is the fair summary, and I would say it to any of them to their face. The team that runs LiveWire today inherited a $2.31 billion valuation, a 100,000-unit promise, and a cost structure built for a company ten times its size. They have cut, sourced, re-priced, rebuilt a network and launched two platforms while doing it. What they do not have is a lineup with volume in it, and what they cannot get is a set of contracts that let them win even if they found one. You cannot execute your way out of cost-plus, take-or-pay, a ninety-day trapdoor, and a secured note held by your own parent. Those were signed above their pay grade, and some of them before most of them arrived.

The final word · Harley-Davidson

Harley didn’t leave. It changed seats.

Strip away the language and here is what the filings describe. In 2021 Harley-Davidson sold the world a $2.31 billion electric motorcycle company and told investors, on a call filed with the SEC, that it would do roughly 100,000 units and almost $1.8 billion in revenue by 2026. In 2026 it is doing 923 units and $31 million, and Harley’s own annual report says it “does not plan to make additional investments in LiveWire beyond the amount outstanding under the Term Loan.”

Between those two sentences, Harley moved from the parent’s chair to the banker’s. It still builds the bikes, at cost-plus. It still charges the services fee. It still floors the dealers through HDFS. It now collects SOFR + 4% on $76.8 million secured on everything in the building, and it holds a services agreement it can end for convenience on ninety days’ notice. It gets paid on the way up, on the way down, and on the way out. The only party in this structure that carries LiveWire’s risk without collecting LiveWire’s fees is the 22% public float — and, through consolidation, Harley’s own shareholders, who absorb about $0.65 a share of it a year from a segment that is not named in their five-year plan.

I ran product at Harley. I know how a program like this gets born, and I know the meeting where it gets quietly starved. None of what is in these filings is illegal, unusual, or even unwise from Harley’s chair. It is simply the sound of a company that has decided, and has written the decision into contracts while saying nothing in a press release. When the 8-K amending the credit agreement lands — and it will — remember that the terms were set in November 2025, and the 386% was just the thing that got everyone to look.

14 — Method & standing

How this was built, and by whom

Author

William Weppner is an independent expert witness and litigation consultant working in electric vehicle and powersports product liability, and the principal of Contact Patch Advisory.

Previously: Product Manager for Touring, CVO and Trike at Harley-Davidson; Sales Planning Lead for the CRF line and planning lead on the Grom at Honda; Product Development Director at Super73; Director of OEM Sales at Sena Technologies; and roles at Amphenol Nova Sensor and LID Technology. Founder of Faction MX, sold to private equity. Expert-level motocross racer.

Method

Primary documents first. Figures come from filed financial statements or are computed from them, and the computation is shown.

Derived figures are labelled. Per-unit economics, trailing-twelve-month revenue and breakeven volumes are arithmetic on filed numbers, identified in the captions.

Fact and opinion are separated. Sections 01–08 are sourced. Sections 09, 10 and 12 are judgment, and say so. Where an interpretation rests on my industry experience rather than a document — as with the undefined term “production” — it is marked as my reading.

No position is held. I hold no long or short position in LiveWire Group, Harley-Davidson, or any company named in this brief, and have no engagement adverse or favourable to them.

Corrections log

Each of the following was asserted in an earlier revision of this analysis and corrected on reading the underlying document. The log is published because a method is only worth what its error-handling is worth.

What was claimedWhat the document said
A U.S. segment size derived by dividing worldwide units by a U.S. retail share.Invalid on its face — worldwide numerator, U.S. denominator. Removed, and replaced with MIC 601cc+ registrations as a sourced denominator.
Average selling price of $13,655 per motorcycle.That divided total segment revenue, including parts and apparel, by motorcycle units. True ASP is $11,483.
A gross loss of $9,517 per motorcycle, presented without qualification.Roughly 87% of it was the year-over-year increase in net realisable value adjustments, not build cost at sale.
The 40% manufacturing clause had lapsed with the 2022 agreement.It is live and appears in the current 10-K. The search that missed it looked for “40%”; the filing spells it “forty percent”.
The 40% clause caps how much production can move to KYMCO.§8.4 lets either party terminate for convenience on 90 days' notice. H-D needs no trigger at all; the 40% route is slower. The clause is evidence of intent, not a cap.
Exhibit 10.2 to the 8-K of 22 May 2026 is an amended Harley-Davidson manufacturing agreement.It is the KYMCO agreement, and its Exhibit A — products, volumes, prices — is redacted under Item 601(b)(10).
Dust Moto was acquired for $375,000.$375K cash, plus $500K of stock at closing, three annual $875K stock instalments, and up to $11.25M of contingent earn-out. Up to $14.75M.
Debt-for-equity conversion is a mechanism available to Harley-Davidson.It was — under the February 2024 facility, which was never drawn. The November 2025 restatement removed the conversion feature.
NYSE compliance was regained on 3 August 2026.No filing says so. The company has announced no return to compliance and the 5 August 10-Q does not mention the notice. Restated as the author’s reading of the Exchange’s month-end cure test against the 31 July close, with the 23 January 2027 cure deadline shown as the filed position.
The ~10,000-unit Grom volume is sourced to MIC registration data.It is not a published statistic and is not reproduced from MIC. It is the author’s own estimate, formed as planning lead on the Grom program at American Honda, and is now labelled as judgment rather than as a cited figure.
The December 2027 obligation is $76.8M.Interest accrues at SOFR + 4.00% compounded semi-annually with nothing payable until maturity. The payoff is nearer $85M.
Q2 2026 purchases were driven by minimum volume commitments.The Harley minimums begin in calendar 2027. Those purchases were discretionary.
Corrections and challenges

If any figure or reading in this brief is wrong, I want to know. Corrections get made in the document, dated, and added to the log above rather than made quietly.

Method & limitations

What this brief does and does not claim

Every figure is drawn from SEC filings, company releases, or manufacturers' published pricing. Derived figures — per-unit economics, trailing-twelve-month revenue, breakeven volumes — are arithmetic on filed numbers and are identified as such in the captions.

This brief does not assert, and no filing states, that Harley-Davidson intends to divest, wind down, or take LiveWire private. No Schedule 13D has ever been filed on LiveWire. Harley-Davidson's sole ownership filing is a Form 3 dated 26 September 2022, filed jointly by ElectricSoul, LLC, Harley-Davidson Motor Company Group, LLC and Harley-Davidson, Inc.

The Master Services Agreement of 23 December 2024 has now been read. “Production” is not a defined term in it — the word appears once, lowercase, in Section 8.3(c). The reading offered in §07 is the author's industry interpretation of an undefined term, identified as such, and is not represented as the agreement's own definition.

One has been closed and corrected. An earlier revision described the exhibit filed 22 May 2026 as an amended Harley-Davidson manufacturing agreement. It is not — it is the KYMCO agreement, and its Exhibit A, containing the products, volumes and prices, is redacted under Item 601(b)(10). Those figures are not public. The Harley-Davidson minimum volume commitments beginning in calendar 2027 are described in the FY2025 10-K; the underlying agreement dates from 26 September 2022 and was amended 14 February 2024.
